r: The course teaches internet research using search engines to collect, evaluate, and validate information, and preparing reports and business documents in Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. These document-preparation and information-synthesis tasks sit among the most-exposed activities in the evidence base: observed-usage data shows office and writing tasks as a prominent share of model use, and controlled writing studies report large time savings and quality gains. That pushes exposure high. This is a terminal literacy course, and the catalog states it does not serve as a prerequisite for CIS 2010, so no foundational-scaffolding cap protects it, and there is no licensure or accreditation lock. At 24 months the realized effect is tempered mainly by adoption lag rather than capability; AI already drafts documents and synthesizes web research competently. Rating Medium, held there by near-term diffusion.

By 2031, AI systems will draft polished reports, build spreadsheets and slide decks, and gather and evaluate web information with little human input, and the instrumental rationale for a course teaching those exact deliverables erodes sharply. Task-exposure research classifies writing and office work as strongly positively associated with AI exposure, and this course's core outputs are precisely those. With no foundational role, since it is explicitly not a prerequisite, and no institutional mandate holding it in place, little caps the rating. The residual competence is knowing how to direct and sanity-check AI-produced documents, a genuinely smaller skill than composing them from scratch. Diffusion of office AI is already broad and will deepen over this horizon. The rating rises to High: the applied work the course builds toward is performed competently by widely available tools with limited human effort.

A decade out, general office-productivity and information-gathering work is substantially performed by AI in the central case, and the execution rationale for basic digital-literacy instruction is largely gone. The instrumental case shifts to verification and direction, evaluating whether AI-generated documents and summaries are accurate, but that is a modest competence relative to the course's content, and the jagged-frontier evidence that unsupervised users can be misled is a hedge, not a foundational cap. Absent any licensure, accreditation, or scaffolding constraint, the rating is High. The hedge is genuine ten-year uncertainty about how basic computer literacy is taught and assessed when AI mediates most document work, and whether some baseline fluency remains expected of every worker. That concerns pedagogy, not whether the applied tasks remain instrumentally necessary to learn here.
CIS 1005.d: This course emphasizes using the Internet and online resources to collect, understand, evaluate, and validate information relating to basic computer literacy and emerging technologies. Using different search terms and search engines, students will find information that describes computer hardware, software, information systems, Web 2.0, and big data, among other information technology topics. They will prepare brief abstracts and ratings of information gathered. Additionally, students will learn to use Word, Excel, and PowerPoint to prepare reports and business documents. This course does not serve as a pre-requisite for CIS 2010.

r: The course teaches operating-system use and an office productivity suite of word processing, spreadsheets, presentation, and database, plus historical, ethical, and cybersecurity context. The productivity-tool tasks are among the most-exposed in the evidence base; observed-usage data ranks office and writing work as a prominent share of model activity. That would push exposure high, but the binding constraint is foundational: CIS 1010, or its screening-test equivalent, is a stated prerequisite for CIS 2010, the gateway to the entire CIS curriculum, making it critical scaffolding. Students cannot meaningfully use, supervise, or build on downstream information-systems coursework without baseline computer fluency. The foundational-scaffolding cap holds the rating at Medium even though AI already performs the document and spreadsheet tasks competently. Rating Medium, capped by its prerequisite role rather than by capability.

By 2031, AI will handle routine document, spreadsheet, and presentation production fluently, and the produce-these-artifacts-yourself rationale weakens considerably. Task-exposure research places office and writing work firmly in the exposed band. Yet the course's role as required substrate for CIS 2010 and the broader major caps the rating at Medium regardless of how automatable basic productivity tasks become: baseline fluency with operating systems, files, and applications remains the precondition for later information-systems study and for supervising AI-mediated office work. The instrumental case shifts from performing the tasks to being literate enough to direct and verify them. The rating holds Medium, with high task-exposure pushing up and foundational scaffolding preventing High. This is the same substrate-role logic that caps introductory computing courses generally.

A decade out, AI performs most basic office and information-management work in the central case, and the execution rationale for introductory computer literacy is substantially eroded. But the course's function as foundational scaffolding for the CIS program persists: some baseline digital competence remains the substrate on which every later course, and any oversight of AI office tools, depends. The rating holds Medium, explicitly capped by foundational role from rising to High. The ten-year uncertainty is pedagogical, namely how and whether introductory computer literacy is taught when AI mediates the tasks, rather than about whether foundational fluency remains instrumentally necessary for students continuing in information systems. The evidence base's verification findings reinforce that literate human oversight of AI-mediated work retains value at this horizon.
CIS 1010.n: September 2026 evidence update. Task automatability (F1) raised at 24 months from 3 to 4. Applied outcome is operating a PC and an office productivity suite (word processing, spreadsheets, presentations, database), i.e., routine office-software execution. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' 2025-35 projections state that AI is likely to reduce demand for office and administrative support occupations (-4.0%, the largest loss of any major group). No rating changed, because the foundational-course cap already binds.
CIS 1010.d: This course is designed for students who wish to use a microcomputer in their academic pursuits and their career. The student will learn how to use a personal computer operating system and an office productivity suite (word processing, spreadsheets, presentation, database). This course also reviews the historical, societal, ethical, cyber security and technological aspects of computers.

r: The course teaches basic internet skills of email, remote login, retrieving online documents and software, and browser-based searching, plus the fundamentals of Web page construction. The search, retrieval, and document tasks are highly exposed office-style work, and web-page coding falls in the single most-exposed category: observed-usage data ranks computer and mathematical work as the largest usage share, and a controlled trial found a 55.8% task-speed gain for developers using AI assistance. That pushes exposure high. The content is also dated, referencing Netscape, and the course is terminal, not a prerequisite for the CIS core, so no foundational cap applies and there is no licensure or accreditation lock. At 24 months the realized effect is limited mainly by adoption rather than capability; AI already builds simple web pages and performs web research competently. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will generate web pages from natural-language descriptions and handle information retrieval end to end, and the instrumental rationale for teaching basic internet use and elementary page construction erodes substantially. Task-exposure research classifies programming and web work as strongly positively associated with exposure, and this course's deliverables are squarely within it. With no foundational role and no institutional mandate holding the course in place, little caps the rating. The residual competence, specifying what a site should do and verifying generated markup, is narrower than hand-building pages. The rating rises to High: the applied work is performed competently by broadly available tools with limited human input, and for content this elementary the erosion is pronounced.

A decade out, generating and deploying basic web content and retrieving online information are substantially automated in the central case, and the execution rationale for elementary web and internet skills is largely gone. The instrumental case shifts toward direction and verification of AI-produced sites, a modest competence relative to the course's content. Absent embodiment, licensure, accreditation, or a scaffolding cap, the rating is High. The hedge is ordinary ten-year uncertainty and the jagged-frontier caution that users who cannot read markup may miss non-obvious errors, a residual verification value rather than a foundational constraint. For an already-dated introductory course, the direction is clear: the applied tasks it teaches are performed competently by AI.
CIS 1080.d: This course is for anyone who uses or wants to access the World Wide Web or use the Internet. Students will master a set of basic skills including using electronic mail, logging-in to remote computers, obtaining online documents and software, and using a browser like Netscape to search and explore the World Wide Web for information. Students will also learn the fundamentals of Web page construction.

r: The course places students in an approved business internship to gain practical, hands-on professional work experience, explore career paths, and build professionalism. The defining activity is embodied and experiential, being present in a workplace, performing real professional work, and developing interpersonal and professional judgment through direct participation. These map to O*NET interpersonal and presence-dependent activities that task-exposure research places well outside AI's reach: a model can draft an intern's deliverables, but it cannot undergo the workplace experience on the student's behalf, which is the course's entire instrumental purpose. There is no capability by which AI substitutes for lived professional immersion. At 24 months the instrumental need is untouched; the low-exposure, high-presence nature of an internship, not any institutional lock, is the binding protection. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI tools will be embedded in the workplaces where students intern, changing the tasks interns perform and observe. But the course exists to develop a student's own embodied professional competence, namely workplace conduct, interpersonal navigation, and firsthand exposure to a career field, through presence, and automation does not perform that formative experience. The embodiment and real-time interpersonal character keep the instrumental case essentially intact; there is no plausible substitution of an AI attending the internship for the student. No licensure gates this general-business internship, but none is needed, because presence is itself the protection. The rating stays Low; AI changes what interns learn to work alongside, not whether they must show up and do the work themselves.

A decade out, even under aggressive capability assumptions, the experiential core of an internship, a student personally acquiring professional competence and career exposure in a live workplace, is not delegable to AI. Models will shape the work environment and the tasks, and the balance of what interns do will shift toward supervising AI-assisted output, but the instrumental purpose of gaining firsthand professional experience remains. The rating stays Low with high confidence. The ten-year uncertainty concerns which tasks fill the internship, not whether embodied workplace immersion retains instrumental value; if anything, employers may weight demonstrated real-world judgment more heavily as routine work automates. Embodiment and presence, not institutional lock-in, hold this course firmly in the low-exposure band.
CIS 1985.d: Approved internships introduce the specific field of business as well as provide an opportunity to gain practical, hands-on professional work experience. Students will learn about the profession, explore related career paths, and increase professionalism.

r: The course introduces information systems from a business perspective, covering hardware and software, ERP systems, business analytics, and cybersecurity, and emphasizing how organizations use IT assets for strategic advantage. The applied work is conceptual and analytical knowledge work: explaining systems, analyzing business-technology fit, and writing about IT strategy, all exposed to AI given that observed-usage data ranks computer and mathematical work as the largest usage category. That pushes exposure up, but the binding constraint is foundational: CIS 2010 is the gateway course and stated prerequisite for essentially the entire CIS curriculum, including 2110, 2200, 2320, 2500, 3270, and 3300, making it critical scaffolding. Students cannot supervise or build on later IS coursework without this conceptual base. The foundational cap holds the rating at Medium despite high content exposure. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will fluently explain information-systems concepts, summarize ERP and analytics topics, and draft IT-strategy analyses, weakening the rationale for delivering this knowledge through a conventional course. Task-exposure research places such analytical and writing work in the exposed band. Yet the course's role as required substrate for the CIS major caps the rating at Medium regardless of how automatable the knowledge delivery becomes: the conceptual grounding is the precondition for every downstream course and for critically directing AI systems in a business context. The instrumental case shifts from acquiring the concepts through instruction to using them to specify and verify AI-supported information-systems work. The rating holds Medium, with exposed content pushing up and foundational scaffolding preventing High.

A decade out, AI delivers and applies information-systems knowledge at a high level in the central case, and the transmission rationale for an introductory survey erodes substantially. But the course's function as foundational scaffolding for the CIS program persists: conceptual fluency about systems, data, and security remains the substrate on which later study and any human oversight of enterprise AI depend. The rating holds Medium, capped by foundational role from going High. The ten-year uncertainty is how the gateway is taught and assessed under ubiquitous AI, not whether the foundational understanding remains instrumentally necessary for students continuing in the major. The evidence indicates it does, increasingly as verification competence for AI-mediated business systems whose failures are non-obvious.
CIS 2010.d: This course is an introduction to information systems from a business perspective. It covers a wide range of information systems, computer hardware and software. Students are introduced to ERP systems, business analytics and cyber security issues for business. Emphasis is placed on how organizations can use their Information technology assets to gain strategic advantage.

r: The course teaches structured design and procedural programming, implementing sequence, selection, and iteration, and developing, testing, and debugging programs across languages and platforms. Coding is the single most-exposed task in the evidence base: observed-usage data makes computer and mathematical work the largest usage category, and a controlled trial recorded a 55.8% developer speed gain with AI assistance. That would push exposure high, but CIS 2110 is critical foundational scaffolding, the stated prerequisite for the entire CIS upper division, including 3030, 3050, 3060, 3145, 3220, 3230, and 3290. Students cannot read, verify, or debug AI-generated code, or succeed in later courses, without programming fundamentals. Mirroring the introductory-programming pattern, the foundational cap holds the rating at Medium at 24 months even though AI already writes introductory procedural code competently. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI coding assistants will handle most routine implementation of the structured-programming tasks this course teaches, and the write-the-code-yourself rationale weakens further. But the jagged-frontier evidence is directly on point: developers who cannot read and debug AI output produce unreliable software, and that verification competence is exactly what these foundations build. As load-bearing scaffolding for every later CIS course, the rating is capped at Medium regardless of how automatable entry-level coding becomes. The instrumental case shifts decisively from writing procedural code to specifying, testing, and validating it, a Medium rather than a High, because the foundational knowledge remains required for that oversight and for the downstream curriculum. The rating holds Medium.

A decade out, AI generates most routine code in the central case, and the developer role centers on specification, architecture, and verification. Introductory programming's execution rationale is substantially eroded, but the conceptual foundation remains necessary to do that higher-order work, to catch the model's non-obvious failures, and to scaffold the whole major. The rating holds Medium, explicitly capped by foundational role from going High. The wide ten-year uncertainty concerns how programming is taught when AI writes the code, not whether computational fundamentals remain instrumentally necessary here; the evidence, especially the jagged-frontier verification findings, indicates they do, as the substrate for supervising AI-generated software. Even as the write-it-yourself rationale disappears, the read-and-verify competence this course builds remains load-bearing for the entire major, which is why the foundational cap binds at Medium rather than releasing to High. Rating Medium.
CIS 2110.n: September 2026 evidence update. Task automatability (F1) raised at 24 months from 3 to 4. Centers on implementing sequence/selection/iteration constructs in procedural languages and writing, testing, and debugging programs, which is routine code production. Stanford's August 2026 payroll update places software developers and computer programmers in the most AI-exposed occupations, where employment of 22-to-25-year-olds is 19% below trend, mainly through reduced hiring; the Bureau of Labor Statistics' 2025-35 projections put computer programmers at -7.3%. Both are descriptive signals, not proof that AI caused the decline. No rating changed, because the foundational-course cap already binds.
CIS 2110.d: This is a problem-solving course in which the tools of structured design are used to design computerized solutions to business problems. Techniques of procedural programming languages are used to implement these designs. Emphasis is placed on the implementation of the three logic constructs in procedural languages: sequence, selection, and iteration. Students will be required to develop, test, and debug programs in one or more languages, using a variety of hardware and operating system platforms.

r: The course covers business intelligence practice: data visualization with industry software, text analytics, social-network analysis, market-basket association mining, and predictive methods such as decision trees, applied to real data. These analytical tasks are highly exposed: observed-usage data ranks computer and mathematical work as the largest usage category, and task-exposure research places quantitative analysts among the most-exposed occupations. That pushes exposure up. The course is applied and largely terminal, with CIS 2010 its only prerequisite and no role as foundational substrate for later required courses, so no scaffolding cap applies, and AACSB provides at most a weak curricular lock. At 24 months the realized effect is limited chiefly by adoption within firms; AI already builds visualizations and fits predictive models competently. Rating Medium, held there by near-term diffusion rather than capability.

By 2031, AI will generate dashboards, run association and predictive analyses, and interpret results in prose with limited human input, and the instrumental rationale for teaching students to execute these BI tasks erodes substantially. Task-exposure research classifies data-analysis work as strongly exposed, and this course's deliverables, namely visualizations, decision-tree models, and textual-data insight, are precisely that. With no foundational role and only a weak AACSB lock, little caps the rating. The residual competence is framing the business question and verifying that model outputs are sound, narrower than performing the full analysis. The rating rises to High: the applied analytical work is performed competently by widely available tools, with human effort concentrated on problem definition.

A decade out, business-intelligence analysis is substantially automated in the central case, with data preparation, visualization, and predictive modeling handled by AI and humans concentrated on problem framing and judgment. The instrumental case for a course teaching BI execution is substantially eroded, shifting toward specifying analyses and verifying results. Absent embodiment, licensure, or a scaffolding cap, the rating is High. The hedge is genuine ten-year uncertainty and the jagged-frontier caution that analysts who cannot interrogate model output may accept subtly wrong conclusions, a residual verification premium rather than a binding constraint. The direction is clear: the applied analytical tasks the course builds toward are performed competently by AI. Rating High.
CIS 2200.d: Business Intelligence is the infrastructure and collection of methods that analyzes data generated by businesses to gain actionable insights. This course covers the practical aspects of the field and intended for all business majors. It covers the principles of data visualization through the use of state-of-the art software, gaining insight to textual data, analyzing social networks and finding associations between items that customers buy together. The course also covers predictive methods such as decision trees. The delivery is practice oriented with emphasis on the application with real life data. The course takes advantage of industry leading software to deliver the material.

r: The course applies statistical inference to business decision-making, covering descriptive statistics, probability, distributions, sampling, point and interval estimation, and hypothesis testing. Statistical analysis is strongly exposed: task-exposure research ranks mathematicians and quantitative analysts among the most-exposed occupations, and observed-usage data makes computer and mathematical work the largest usage category. That pushes exposure up. The course is a largely terminal quantitative service course, with MTH 1320 its prerequisite and only an alternative-prerequisite relationship to CIS 3300, so no strong scaffolding cap binds, and AACSB provides at most a weak lock. At 24 months the effect is tempered by adoption; AI already computes and explains statistical procedures competently, though translating them into defensible business decisions still draws human oversight. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will fluently perform and explain the full inferential toolkit, from estimation to hypothesis tests and their business interpretation, weakening the rationale for teaching students to execute these procedures. Task-exposure research places quantitative work firmly in the exposed band. With no binding foundational role and only a weak AACSB lock, little caps the rating. The residual value is framing the inferential question, checking assumptions, and interpreting results in context, competence that shrinks relative to hand-computation. The jagged-frontier evidence supplies a hedge: users who cannot judge whether a test was appropriate may trust flawed output. On balance the rating rises to High, as the applied statistical work becomes broadly automatable while defensible interpretation remains a narrower human task.

A decade out, statistical analysis for business decisions is substantially performed by AI in the central case, with humans concentrated on posing questions and vetting conclusions. The instrumental case for a course teaching inferential execution is substantially eroded, shifting toward specification and verification. Absent embodiment, licensure, or a foundational cap, the rating is High, hedged by ten-year uncertainty and by the real verification premium the jagged-frontier findings imply for statistical judgment: knowing when a model's inference is unsound is not itself automated away. But that residual is narrower than the course's applied content, and the direction is clear: the quantitative tasks the course builds toward are competently automatable. Rating High.
CIS 2300.d: This is a course in the application of statistical inference and translation of quantitative data into information which can be used in business decision-making. This course will cover the topics of descriptive statistics, probability theory, probability distributions, sampling distributions, point estimates, confidence intervals, and tests of hypotheses, in the context of management decision-making skills needed by industry.

r: The course teaches descriptive and predictive analytics for business, covering data collection and organization, descriptive and inferential statistics, probability, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and regression, using manual and software calculation, with emphasis on communicating findings to stakeholders. These analytical and reporting tasks are strongly exposed: observed-usage data ranks computer and mathematical work as the largest usage category, and task-exposure research places quantitative analysts among the most-exposed. That pushes exposure up. The course is applied and largely terminal, with a math course and CIS 2010 as prerequisites and no role as required substrate for later courses, so no scaffolding cap binds, and AACSB is a weak lock at most. At 24 months adoption, not capability, limits the effect; AI already runs regressions and drafts stakeholder-ready interpretations competently. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will perform regression and predictive analyses, generate the software output, and draft the stakeholder communication the course emphasizes, with limited human input. Task-exposure research classifies both the quantitative analysis and the writing-up of results as exposed activities, and a controlled writing study found large time and quality gains from AI assistance. With no foundational role and only weak AACSB grounding, little caps the rating. The residual competence, framing the analysis and verifying that results and their communication are sound, is narrower than executing the full workflow. The rating rises to High: the applied analytics-and-reporting work is performed competently by broadly available tools, with human effort concentrated on framing and verification.

A decade out, predictive analytics and its business reporting are substantially automated in the central case, with humans concentrated on question framing and accountability for conclusions. The instrumental case for a course teaching the analytics-and-communication workflow is substantially eroded, shifting toward specification and verification. Absent embodiment, licensure, or a scaffolding cap, the rating is High. The hedge is ten-year uncertainty and the jagged-frontier caution that decision-makers who cannot interrogate a model may propagate subtly wrong analyses to stakeholders, a residual verification value rather than a binding constraint. The direction is clear: the applied statistical and reporting tasks the course builds toward, from regression through the stakeholder-facing communication of results, are performed competently by AI with narrowing human involvement. Rating High.
CIS 2320.d: The course is designed to provide students with an introduction to the fundamentals of descriptive and predictive analytics within the context of statistics for business. Through a combination of lectures, discussions, and practical exercises, students develop a solid understanding of the key statistical concepts and techniques used in various business situations. The course covers a wide range of topics including data collection, organization, analysis, and interpretation using descriptive and inferential statistics. Students learn how to use statistical techniques such as probability theory, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing and regression analysis to make informed business decisions. Emphasis is placed on developing the skills necessary to apply statistical methods in a practical context - using manual and software calculations - including the ability to analyze real-world data sets and effectively communicate findings to stakeholders. By the end of the course, students should be able to use statistical techniques to solve complex business problems and make data-driven decisions.

r: This is a security-awareness course for non-CIS/CYB majors, covering securing systems and networks, protecting personal and organizational data, handling risk and ethical dilemmas, and understanding computer crime, policy, and law. The applied work is largely advisory and knowledge-based: assessing hygiene, drafting policy, and applying best practices, which are exposed to AI. Security does carry an adversarial, high-error-cost character that raises verification burden, but at the awareness level this course targets, the tasks are routine enough that AI advises competently. There is no licensure or accreditation lock, and the course is a terminal non-major elective with only CIS 2010 preceding it, so no scaffolding cap binds. At 24 months adoption tempers the effect; AI already explains and recommends baseline security practices well. Rating Medium, with the verification character of security noted as a partial hedge.

By 2031, AI assistants will competently advise on personal and organizational security hygiene, draft policies, and explain threats and legal obligations, weakening the rationale for a dedicated awareness course. Task-exposure research places such advisory and writing work in the exposed band. No foundational role or institutional mandate holds the course in place. The countervailing factor is real, since security is adversarial and the jagged-frontier evidence warns that users who over-trust AI in a threat context can be misled, sustaining some human verification value. But for awareness-level content aimed at non-majors, that residual is limited. On balance the rating rises to High, as the applied security-guidance tasks become broadly automatable. Confidence is medium given the verification-burden judgment.

A decade out, routine security guidance and policy work are substantially automated in the central case. The instrumental case for an awareness course erodes toward knowing enough to recognize when AI security advice is wrong in an adversarial setting, a genuine but narrow residual that the jagged-frontier findings support. Absent embodiment, licensure, or a scaffolding cap, the rating is High, more heavily hedged than the analytics courses because security's high error cost and adversarial nature could sustain more human involvement than a pure capability read implies. Ten-year uncertainty is real here. The direction still points to High: for non-specialist security literacy, the applied advisory tasks the course builds toward are competently performed by AI. Confidence medium.
CIS 2500.d: This course is designed to teach the principles and practices that all computing users need to keep sensitive information secure, both at work and at home. By introducing students to security theory and presenting best practices, the course will show students both the importance of protecting data and the associated techniques. Topics covered include how to secure systems, protecting personal data, organizational resources, securing computer networks, how to handle risks and ethical dilemmas, computer crime, policies and laws, and how to implement safe Internet usage. This course is not intended for CIS and CYB majors.

r: The course develops business websites end to end: planning a site, writing specifications, and applying code in a code-centric editor with a supplemental graphical tool. Web development is at the center of the most-exposed task category: observed-usage data makes computer and mathematical work the largest usage share, and a controlled trial found a 55.8% task-speed gain for developers using AI, with web front-end generation among the capabilities models already perform fluently and that are widely deployed. The course is an upper-division elective with CIS 2110 as its prerequisite, no foundational-scaffolding role, and no licensure or accreditation lock. Unlike introductory programming, no foundational cap restrains the rating. Even at 24 months, AI competently generates functional web pages from specifications with broad tool availability. Rating High.

By 2031, AI will generate complete, styled, interactive websites from natural-language specifications, and the instrumental rationale for teaching hand-coding of business web pages erodes substantially. Task-exposure research classifies programming as strongly positively associated with exposure. With no foundational role and no institutional mandate, nothing caps the rating. The residual competence, specifying requirements and verifying generated code and design, is real but narrower than building sites by hand, and the jagged-frontier evidence indicates developers who cannot read the output risk shipping subtle defects. The rating stays High: the applied web-development work is performed competently by AI with limited human input, and diffusion in this domain is already advanced relative to most occupational software.

A decade out, web development is substantially performed by AI in the central case, with humans concentrated on specification, integration, and verification. The instrumental case for a course teaching site construction is substantially eroded. Absent embodiment, licensure, accreditation, or a scaffolding cap, the rating is High. The hedge is ten-year uncertainty and the residual verification premium held by developers who can read and correct AI-generated markup and logic, a real but specialist competence smaller than the course's full applied content. As an upper-division skills course lacking any foundational cap, and covering exactly the front-end coding that models generate most fluently, its instrumental case is squarely exposed. The direction is clear and the rating holds High, hedged only by the specialist verification residue.
CIS 3030.n: September 2026 evidence update. Task automatability (F1) raised at 24 months from 4 to 5, 5 years from 4 to 5. Students code business web pages in a code-centric editor, which is routine web page building. Stanford's August 2026 payroll update places software developers and computer programmers in the most AI-exposed occupations, where employment of 22-to-25-year-olds is 19% below trend, mainly through reduced hiring; the Bureau of Labor Statistics' 2025-35 projections put computer programmers at -7.3%. Both are descriptive signals, not proof that AI caused the decline. No rating changed, because an existing cap already binds.
CIS 3030.d: This is a course in business Web page development. Specifically, the student will learn how to plan the development of a Web site, compose Web site specifications, apply coding to the development of any kind of Web site, and find and use development resources. The student will use a leading code-centric text editor to aid in all course Web page development projects. The student will also be introduced to a leading graphical editing tool for supplemental use.

r: The course teaches the analysis phase of systems development: requirements definition, modeling, feasibility, project planning and management, and documentation, under business drivers such as security, privacy, and collaboration. The applied deliverables are analytical and written, namely requirements documents, models, and feasibility analyses, which are exposed to AI given that observed-usage data ranks computer and mathematical work highest and that writing tasks show large productivity gains in controlled studies. Requirements work retains a stakeholder-facing element, but it is largely digital rather than embodied. The course is an upper-division elective with CIS 2110 as prerequisite, no foundational-scaffolding role, and no licensure lock. At 24 months adoption tempers the effect; AI already drafts requirements and models competently, while eliciting and validating them still draws on human judgment. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will draft requirements specifications, generate process and data models, and produce feasibility and planning documentation with limited human input, and the instrumental rationale for teaching students to author these artifacts erodes substantially. Task-exposure research places analytical writing and documentation in the exposed band. With no foundational role and only a weak AACSB lock, little caps the rating. The residual competence, eliciting genuine needs from stakeholders and verifying that models and requirements are correct and complete, is real but narrower than performing the full analysis. The rating rises to High: the applied systems-analysis deliverables, from requirements documents to feasibility studies, are produced competently by AI, with human effort concentrated on elicitation and validation.

A decade out, systems-analysis documentation and modeling are substantially automated in the central case, with humans concentrated on stakeholder judgment and validating requirements against real needs. The instrumental case for a course teaching the analysis phase is substantially eroded, shifting toward specification and verification. Absent embodiment, licensure, or a scaffolding cap, the rating is High, hedged by ten-year uncertainty and by the durable interpersonal element of requirements elicitation, since negotiating what stakeholders actually want is less automatable than documenting it. But that interpersonal residual is a fraction of the course's content, and it does not preserve the full instrumental case for teaching the analysis phase. The direction is clear: the applied analytical and documentation tasks are competently performed by AI. Rating High.
CIS 3050.d: This course covers the basic concepts of an information system and systems analysis tools and techniques necessary to develop requirements for a business information system. Students will concentrate on systems analysis using current methodologies, technologies, and available tools of analysis, as well as an examination of the effect on systems analysis by business drivers such as globalization, security, privacy, ethics, and collaboration. The course will focus on the analysis phase including requirements definition, modeling, feasibility, project planning and management, and documentation.

r: The course covers database design, development, implementation, and manipulation, building designs from user requirements, implementing them with a 4GL tool, and touching distributed databases, concurrency, data warehousing, and data mining. Database and query work is coding-adjacent and highly exposed: observed-usage data ranks computer and mathematical work as the largest usage category, and a controlled trial found a 55.8% developer speed gain with AI, with SQL and schema generation among tasks models perform fluently. The course is an upper-division elective with CIS 2110 as prerequisite, no foundational-scaffolding role, and no licensure lock. At 24 months adoption tempers the effect, and schema design still involves architectural judgment; AI already writes queries and generates schemas from requirements competently. Rating Medium, limited chiefly by near-term diffusion.

By 2031, AI will design normalized schemas from requirements, write and optimize queries, and configure warehousing and mining pipelines with limited human input, and the instrumental rationale for teaching hand-implementation of databases erodes substantially.
